newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Karadzic name underlines complexity of Bosnia poll.
newsitem.headline: Karadzic name underlines complexity of Bosnia poll.

text.p: Radovan Karadzic is standing in Bosnia's election after all, but relieved international organisers insist they were not facing another case of Serb defiance.
The candidate only shares the name of the notorious Bosnian Serb warlord and indicted war criminal banned from participation in the September 14 poll.
"We have taken careful note, this is not THE Radovan Karadzic," Agota Kuperman, spokeswoman of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), told reporters.
She added OSCE checks had revealed his full name was Radovan M Karadzic and no breach of election rules had taken place.
The second Karadzic is a member of the same Bosnian Serb Democratic Party (SDS) and hopes to win a seat in a new countrywide House of Representatives.
"One thing is certain, he's sure of a high vote," quipped one independent election observer.

The incident neatly underlined the problems facing the OSCE in organising next Saturday's elections for a host of regional and national presidencies and assemblies, considered essential if the Dayton peace accords which ended the war are to last.
Robert Frowick, head of the Bosnia OSCE mission, has billed the polls "the most complicated election of the century".
Another major problem facing the organisers is how to allow thousands of displaced people to vote in home areas they were forced to flee during the 3-1/2 year war.

NATO and the United Nations have drawn up a controversial plan to escort them over ethnic boundary lines via 19 selected routes to vote in their former home districts and make sure they are free from harassment.

Carl Bildt, the international peace coordinator in Bosnia, said on Monday the "traffic management" plan would be a feat to carry out, not least because of the limited road infrastructure and the dangers of "gridlock".
Roughly 65,000 people are expected to cross from federation territory and perhaps 100,000 from Serb-held Bosnia and Serbia.

Critics say the plan will curb free movement and the ability to vote freely, safely and privately by reserving the routes for vehicles carrying at least eight people and relying on state party-run bus services to transport refugees.
"The major concern we have with the transport arrangement is political control over bus lines, control on whom will be allowed onto buses," Bildt said.

"That's an obvious risk against which we must be prepared to take action." He said international officials were trying to iron out the issue with Moslem-Croat and Serb authorities to ensure the transport arrangements were politically neutral.

Over the next few days, some 980 international foreign supervisors are due to arrive in the country to monitor the polls. Working in teams of two, they will visit as many of the 4,400 polling stations as possible.
Critics point out that over three-quarters of the supervisors will have had no previous experience of Bosnia. Many polling stations are certain not be visited, they say.

Election organisers received one piece of good news on Monday when the man charged with certifying whether the poll is "free and fair" said he had no reason to believe the correct procedures would not be followed.
Ed Van Thijn, coordinator of the international observers, said he would make a preliminary statement 48 hours after the poll and a final statement one week later.
"I am very satisfied," he told reporters following rumours he was considering resignation after coming under pressure to endorse the poll before the final results were announced.
